message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs that affect health or safety must be made promptly. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the rent). | • Keep receipts or bank records of payments.
• If you’re late, communicate with the landlord and negotiate a payment plan if needed. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants can terminate with **30 days’ notice**.
• Tenants with a fixed‑term lease can break it only if the landlord breaches the lease or if the lease contains a “break clause.” | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail).
• Keep a copy of the notice for your records. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry to the landlord in writing. | | **Landlord Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries and verify that the notice was given. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public housing assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Privacy** | • Landlords cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • Document any unauthorized entries. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlords must keep common areas clean and safe. | • Report issues in writing; if unresolved, you may withhold rent or seek a repair order. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but only after giving written notice and a reasonable deadline. | • Keep receipts and a written notice to the landlord. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (30 days) or a **Notice to Vacate** (30 days for nonpayment or lease violation).
• If the landlord files an unlawful detainer suit, you’ll receive a summons and have 10 days to respond. | • Respond promptly in writing.
• Attend the court hearing; bring evidence of your compliance and any lease terms. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for damages, recover unpaid rent, or seek a court order to compel repairs. | • Consider small claims court (up to $20,000) or civil court for larger claims. | | **Fair Housing** | • Landlords must comply with federal and state fair housing laws. | • File complaints with HUD or TCHR if you suspect discrimination. | #### Quick Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, receipts, emails, and any written communication with the landlord. 2. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific notice periods for rent increases, lease termination, and landlord entry. 3. **Use Official Channels** – For disputes, start with a written notice to the landlord. If unresolved, contact TDHCA, TCHR, or HUD, or consider legal action. 4. **Seek Legal Aid** – If you’re unsure about your rights or need representation, consult a local tenant‑rights organization or a lawyer specializing in landlord‑tenant law. --- **Disclaimer:** This overview is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may affect your rights. For personalized guidance, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
